source.title: ScopeSAE: Model-Scope Feature Discovery with Interpretable Layer Selection
source.authors: Qing-Wen Zeng; Ze-Hao Fu; Shu-Yu Meng; Ling-Han Huang; Jia-Yi Zhang; Chenglin Wu; Ling Chen; Hua-Ming Chen

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether SAE-derived features have stable referents and refines that account: ScopeSAE features are mostly concentrated in one selected layer, but their referents are per-feature rather than dictionary-wide. It also reports LLM SAE feature-discovery results, but does not test toy-model superposition.
record.gate_note: The paper cites superposition as background and uses SAEs to discover and evaluate LLM features. It does not test toy networks, feature sparsity-dependent geometric transitions, neuron polysemanticity, or whether feature directions are one-dimensional versus multidimensional. Rows cover its reported LLM SAE feature-discovery metrics and its explicit feature-layer stability analysis. Other reported behavioral, reconstruction, steering, and compute results do not measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is an SAE methods paper. It assumes superposition and SAE feature recovery as motivation and benchmarks its own ScopeSAE against other SAEs on feature count, GPT-4o interpretability, utilization and decoder cosine. It does not test whether LLMs hold superposed sparse features or whether dictionary features are the model's canonical units. The layer-concentration analysis checks ScopeSAE's own interpretive contract, not the stability of features across dictionaries.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but it omits the headline result. The authors' main claim is a 'reconstruction-better-than-original' effect: ScopeSAE write-back lowers next-token cross-entropy (DeltaCE −0.20 at k=64). They attribute this to removing the prediction-orthogonal residual, enabled by the prediction-relevant subspace. They also claim better feature count, interpretability, utilization, redundancy and steering consistency than baselines. They note a per-feature rather than dictionary-wide layer referent.
record.recipe_differences: Different from Toy Models of Superposition: trains an SAE on LLM token-layer activations selected by gradient attribution; it does not use a toy-network superposition setup or test the original toy-model geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature results vary by SAE method and model; ScopeSAE's interpretability score is reported across sparsity levels k∈[48,72]. The per-feature layer-concentration analysis uses a sample of 100 features.

fits_no_version.finding: The interpretable feature count depends strongly on the SAE training distribution: 5,319 for ScopeSAE vs 2,916 for TopK at the same dictionary size. Per-layer TopK SAEs give 2,675–3,135.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The number of interpretable SAE features recovered from an LLM depends on the SAE method and modeling subspace.

fits_no_version.finding: 87% of 100 sampled ScopeSAE features draw selected states from a single layer; 95% draw at least 80% from one layer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Features learned over cross-layer selected states mostly anchor to one layer.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2026 (stated in the paper as the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems)
record.problems: The interpretability evaluation samples 100 features per method and relies on GPT-4o, with human verification also reported on 100 features. Most feature metrics do not report uncertainty; the paper checklist states that formal error bars are not reported. Feature extraction metrics do not establish that the dictionary is complete or canonical.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were omitted for the 60-row limit. Excluded reported metrics that do not measure the claim versions, including reconstruction cross-entropy, residual-gradient alignment, feature steering win rates, intervention side effects, and training cost.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
No neuron polysemanticity or capacity allocation.
Feature recovery by SAEs is assumed and used to compare methods; neuron-level spreading is not measured.
No comparison of feature identity across dictionaries, seeds or methods; completeness and canonicality are not tested.
Not tested; the 1-D and k-D analyses concern the prediction-gradient subspace, not feature dimensionality.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from T5/tests to T4. The rows are the study's own method benchmarked against baselines, with superposition and SAE feature recovery taken as given. The original source (Toy Models) is cited only as background.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, sparse-feature overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometric arrangement are tested.
The paper does not measure neuron polysemanticity or test whether important features get dedicated dimensions while others share capacity.
The paper does not investigate polysemantic neurons or alternative causes of polysemanticity.

Tests SAE-extracted feature count and GPT-4o-scored interpretability in LLMs; it does not measure how a feature is distributed across ordinary neurons or establish that the dictionary recovers all model features.

Tests concentration of ScopeSAE feature selections by layer for 100 sampled features. Does not establish completeness, canonicality, or stability across different SAE dictionaries, training runs, or methods.

The paper studies a one-dimensional prediction-gradient attribution direction and some higher-dimensional prediction subspaces, not whether the model's represented features themselves are one-dimensional or multidimensional.

relation.reason: The experiments evaluate SAE feature quality, dictionary efficiency, reconstruction and interventions rather than whether superposition holds or SAE features are complete, stable and canonical.

tranche.reason: The study uses superposition and sparse dictionary recovery as motivation and benchmarks its own SAE method; its results do not directly test a listed claim version.

source_check.notes: These are method-performance rows, with no direct claim-version verdict warranted. Uncertainty is available in Appendix O, Table 17: over three training seeds, next-token-selection feature count is 5319 ± 46, utilization 99.8 ± 0.08%, and decoder cosine similarity 0.0202 ± 0.00007 (mean ± standard deviation).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: ScopeSAE features on the tested Llama and Qwen instruct models
reader_labels.reason: The study reports thousands of interpretable SAE features, a GPT-4o interpretability score of 4.44 at k=64, and high dictionary utilization; the reported feature counts also extend to Qwen and larger Llama models (R1, R4, R8, R14–R16). This supports SAE-recoverable features, not neuron-wise spreading or completeness.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Layer selections are entirely from one layer for 87% of sampled features and at least 80% concentrated in one layer for 95%, but the authors describe referents as per-feature and not dictionary-wide, and do not establish completeness or canonicality (R17–R18).
